Summarize the methodology of The Impact of the Feed Rate and the Binder Concentration on the Morphology of Spray-Dried Alumina–Polymer Nanocomposites.

Paper profile:
Title: The Impact of the Feed Rate and the Binder Concentration on the Morphology of Spray-Dried Alumina–Polymer Nanocomposites
Keywords: spray-drying, optimization, process–product relationship, polymer composite, particle technology, image processing, parametric stochastic modeling
Topics: Spray-drying of alumina–polymer nanocomposites, Effects of feed rate and binder concentration on granule morphology, Granule porosity and nano-pore volume/size characterization, Inline and offline particle imaging for morphology analysis, Process–structure relationships and model-based process control
Methods: Spray-drying a suspension of nano-alumina and PVP-30 in distilled water; Droplet size and velocity measurement using a HiWatch system; Inline SOPAT imaging for granule morphology analysis; Offline scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for morphology characterization; Mercury intrusion porosimetry to quantify pore volume and pore size; Parametric stochastic modeling (for interpretable process–product relationships)
Materials or datasets: Spherical alumina powder (ASFP-20, Denka Co. Ltd., Tokyo, Japan); Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP-30) binder; Distilled water (suspension medium); Droplet size/velocity distributions (HiWatch measurements); Inline granule images (SOPAT imaging system); SEM images of raw and spray-dried material; Mercury intrusion porosimetry data (pore volume and pore size)
Results: Higher feed rates produced larger droplets with faster velocities, affecting final dried-product morphology.; Increasing binder concentration produced a more compact granule morphology with lower nano-pore volume.; Higher feed rates produced larger granules with larger nano-pore volume.
Conclusions: Feed rate and binder concentration have distinct, systematic impacts on granule size, morphology, and nano-pore volume in spray-dried alumina–PVP nanocomposites.; Correlating inline morphology imaging with offline porosity characterization supports establishing process–structure relationships useful for future control strategies.
Limitations: The experimental investigation focused on two process parameters (feed rate and binder concentration) while other process parameters were held constant.; The study focus was on pore sizes roughly within the micro/meso/macropore range of interest (especially below about 200 nm).

Summarize the methodology of Statistical Analysis and Modeling of the 3D Morphology and Texture of Lunar Regolith Simulants.

Paper profile:
Title: Statistical Analysis and Modeling of the 3D Morphology and Texture of Lunar Regolith Simulants
Keywords: 3D image data, X-ray micro-CT, regolith simulant, particle descriptor, parametric stochastic model
Topics: 3D morphology and texture characterization of lunar regolith simulants, Comparison of simulant particle morphology to actual lunar regolith, Multivariate distributions of particle size and shape descriptors, Parametric modeling of multivariate non-Gaussian descriptor vectors, Digital twin / stochastic 3D modeling for virtual materials testing and simulations
Methods: 3D tomographic imaging via micro computed tomography (X-ray micro-CT); Quantification of size and shape descriptors from 3D image data; Multivariate statistical analysis of correlated morphological descriptors; Parametric models for multivariate non-Gaussian probability distributions of descriptor vectors; Comparative analysis across multiple mare and highlands simulants and lunar regolith samples
Materials or datasets: 3D X-ray micro-CT image data of actual lunar regolith particles (three different samples) (regolith.pdf p.1, p.2); 3D X-ray micro-CT image data of seven regolith simulants: CSM-LHT-1, OB1A, LHS-1 (highlands); JSC-1A, LMS-1, OPRL2N, CSM-LMT-1 (mare) (regolith.pdf p.1, p.2)
Results: Large differences in particle morphology are observed both within regolith simulants and between simulants and actual lunar regolith. (regolith.pdf p.1)
Conclusions: Commonly used regolith simulants show substantial morphological differences relative to lunar regolith, motivating development of simulants with more accurate particle morphologies for mechanical-property experiments. (regolith.pdf p.1); Statistically representative digital models of lunar regolith morphology can serve as inputs for numerical simulations of morphology-driven mechanical behavior under lunar conditions. (regolith.pdf p.1)
Limitations: Large-scale experimental investigations of lunar-regolith mechanical properties are currently unfeasible on the Moon, and reproducing lunar conditions on Earth requires elaborate setups (e.g., parabolic flights or drop towers). (regolith.pdf p.2); Large quantities of lunar regolith are unavailable for mechanical experiments, and the applicability of existing simulants is questionable. (regolith.pdf p.2); Particle-size and shape effects on regolith rheology have not yet been thoroughly characterized for lunar regolith particles. (regolith.pdf p.1)
